title: One initial lottery between two deterministic care policies suffices
scope: Alternative exact implementation of the source's finite discounted response model with one expected present-value financing constraint.
significance: Proves an optimal care policy can be implemented by committing initially to a lottery over at most two deterministic stationary rules, including the expected-finance caveat and sharp necessity.
body:
# One initial lottery between two deterministic care policies

The manuscript proves that one occupied state needs randomization at most. A complementary implementation is available under its same response-reduction and expected-financing assumptions: an optimal policy can be selected by a single initial lottery between at most two deterministic stationary policies. The lottery then remains fixed over the entire realized care history.

First omit the financing inequality and let \(\mathcal X\) be the source's nonnegative discounted occupation polytope. Its extreme points correspond to deterministic stationary policies on occupied states. Here is a direct check. At an extreme occupation point, let \(n_+\) be the number of occupied states and \(k\) the number of positive state-action coordinates. As in the source's proof, flow rows outside occupied states vanish on these coordinates. If \(k>n_+\), a nonzero null perturbation preserves all flows and, in both sufficiently small signs, nonnegativity. This contradicts extremality. Since every occupied state requires one action, \(k=n_+\), hence exactly one action per occupied state. Complete the rule arbitrarily at unoccupied states.

A bounded polytope is the convex hull of its finitely many vertices. Denote the corresponding deterministic stationary policies by \(d=1,\ldots,M\), with discounted welfare and outlay
\[
V_d=\frac{\sum r x_d}{1-\beta},\qquad
C_d=\frac{\sum G x_d}{1-\beta}.
\]
Every history-dependent admissible policy therefore has the same welfare-cost pair as an initial lottery with probabilities \(\alpha_d\):
\[
V=\sum_d\alpha_dV_d,\quad C=\sum_d\alpha_dC_d,\quad
\alpha_d\ge0,\quad\sum_d\alpha_d=1.
\tag{A}
\]
Conversely, drawing a policy once and following it forever is itself an admissible history-dependent randomized policy. Its occupation measure is the corresponding convex combination by linearity of expectation. The source's response reduction is essential: future-policy anticipation cannot alter the stipulated response law after the initial draw.

The financed problem is thus a finite linear program in \(\alpha\), with one normalization equality and one expected-cost inequality. An optimal extreme point has at most two positive coordinates when the budget binds, and at most one when it is slack. The proof is the same nullspace argument: more positive weights than active equalities permit opposite feasible perturbations. Consequently at most two deterministic rules suffice.

If the two selected policies have \(C_1<B<C_2\), the exact lottery is
\[
\alpha_1=\frac{C_2-B}{C_2-C_1},\qquad
\alpha_2=\frac{B-C_1}{C_2-C_1}.
\]
Their expected expenditure equals \(B\). At an endpoint or equal costs, a deterministic policy may suffice. Costs may be negative because the source allows net receipts; no nonnegativity assumption is needed for the convex-hull argument.

Randomization can be necessary. Take one absorbing need state with two legal packages. Let \(\beta\in(0,1)\); package zero has per-period welfare and outlay zero, while package one has both equal to \(1-\beta\). The two deterministic stationary policies have welfare-cost pairs \((0,0)\) and \((1,1)\). At budget \(B\in(0,1)\), mixing them with probability \(B\) on package one attains welfare \(B\), whereas the only feasible deterministic rule has welfare zero.

This implementation does not promise that each initially selected policy separately meets the budget: the expensive branch can exceed \(B\). It is valid precisely because finance is an expected present-value constraint backed by the source's outside fiscal account. Requiring solvency separately in every branch would exclude that lottery and change the problem.

The result preserves legal need verification, specified family responses and net fiscal accounting. It does not establish a forward-looking family reduction, identify untried packages, or claim that initial randomization is administratively preferred to the source's one-state lottery.

title: Backward support-function computation for the joint erosion-output region
scope: Exact dynamic-programming computation of sharp support values in the source's finite rectangular transition model.
significance: Replaces the full occupancy optimization for each joint direction with two backward sequences of rowwise linear programs and proves vertex-row witness attainability.
body:
# Backward support computation for the joint erosion-output region

The manuscript identifies a compact joint polytope for the first-loss probability and terminal log-output contrast. Its support values can also be computed by backward recursion, retaining the joint outcome tradeoff while avoiding a single large flow program. Every resulting support point has a witness using extreme transition rows.

Fix real direction weights \(v_1,v_2\) and define the common terminal reward
\[
f(x)=v_1R(x)+v_2\ell_h(x).
\]
For the treatment regime set \(U_h(x)=f(x)\), and recursively define
\[
U_s(x)=\max_{k\in\mathcal K_s^a(x)}
             \sum_yk(y)U_{s+1}(y).
\tag{A}
\]
For the baseline set \(L_h(x)=f(x)\) and
\[
L_s(x)=\min_{k\in\mathcal K_s^{a_0}(x)}
             \sum_yk(y)L_{s+1}(y).
\tag{B}
\]
Then the exact sharp support value of the source's joint region in direction \((v_1,v_2)\) is
\[
h(v_1,v_2)=\sum_x\pi(x)\{U_0(x)-L_0(x)\}.
\tag{C}
\]

For an upper-bound proof, take any admitted treatment kernels. Backward conditioning shows that their expected terminal reward conditional on \(X_s=x\) is at most \(U_s(x)\): it holds at \(h\), and averaging the next-date bound under an admissible row is no larger than the row maximum in (A). The analogous induction bounds every baseline expected reward below by \(L_s(x)\). Integrating over the common initial law proves the bound (C).

For attainability, each row polytope is nonempty and compact, so its finite linear objective attains its extremum. Choose a maximizing row in (A) for every treatment state and date, and a minimizing row in (B) for every baseline state and date. Rectangular compatibility admits all these choices simultaneously, including across the two regimes. Backward induction then makes every inequality an equality. Thus one pair of kernel sequences attains (C). At zero-occupancy states the chosen rows remain admissible but do not affect the target.

Moreover a linear functional on a nonempty polytope attains its optimum at a vertex. Each selected row may therefore be chosen at an extreme point of its permitted row polytope. This gives an explicit witness for each sharp support value. It does not mean the transition is deterministic in its next state: a vertex of a row-restriction polytope can itself be a nondegenerate probability distribution.

The complete joint region is recovered as
\[
\{(\theta,\gamma):v_1\theta+v_2\gamma\le h(v_1,v_2)
\text{ for every }(v_1,v_2)\in\mathbb R^2\}.
\]
Inclusion follows from (C); separation of a point from the compact convex identified polytope proves the converse. Using only the four coordinate directions gives a rectangle and generally discards the dependence between erosion and output already illustrated in the manuscript.

For a fixed direction, the method uses two rowwise linear programs per state and date, followed by weighted sums. With explicitly described rational row polytopes and rational terminal values, the recursion remains an exact finite linear-optimization procedure. It makes no runtime claim for implicit exponentially described states or row restrictions.

The independence of rows is substantive. A shared political-incentive parameter can prevent a row that is worst at one state from coexisting with a row selected elsewhere. In that setting (A)–(C) supply an outer support bound but are not automatically sharp; the common parameter must remain in the optimization. Similarly the first-loss flag must remain in the state, so redemocratization does not erase an earlier transition.

This is a computational characterization of the declared population region. It does not certify exchangeability of actual reforms, estimate political responses, or turn population bounds into confidence intervals. No external source or unexecuted numerical result is invoked.

title: Sharp longitudinal health-completion bounds under bounded annual changes
scope: Refinement of the source's missing-health welfare bounds using an explicitly supplied Lipschitz restriction on quality indices during life.
significance: Constructs simultaneously attainable whole-trajectory completion envelopes and propagates them into sharp net-health-benefit intervals without survivor conditioning.
body:
# Sharp health-completion bounds with bounded annual changes

The manuscript's missing-health bounds allow each unobserved live quality index to range independently over \([0,1]\). If a substantive annual-change restriction is available, the longitudinal structure can tighten those bounds while preserving sharpness. It must be imposed explicitly; it does not follow from missingness or from complete vital-status records.

For a beneficiary and regime, let \(\mathcal T\subseteq\{1,\ldots,5\}\) be the dates alive, with survival fully observed. Let \(\mathcal O\subseteq\mathcal T\) be dates with observed health indices \(q_s\). Fix a supplied \(L\ge0\) and require
\[
0\le q_t\le1,\qquad |q_t-q_s|\le L|t-s|
\quad(t,s\in\mathcal T).
\tag{A}
\]
There is no restriction linking a post-death zero health contribution to the pre-death quality index. Death remains an outcome, not an imputed quality measurement.

Observed values must satisfy (A) among themselves. If they do not, the maintained completion class is empty. If \(\mathcal O\ne\varnothing\), define for each live date
\[
\ell_t=\max\{0,\max_{s\in\mathcal O}(q_s-L|t-s|)\},\qquad
u_t=\min\{1,\min_{s\in\mathcal O}(q_s+L|t-s|)\}.
\tag{B}
\]
If no live quality value is observed, use \(\ell_t=0,u_t=1\). Every admissible trajectory lies between these envelopes, by comparison with every observation.

Both entire envelope trajectories are themselves admissible. Each function \(t\mapsto q_s\pm L|t-s|\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz; maxima and minima of finitely many functions sharing that constant retain it, as does clipping to the constant range endpoints. The observed consistency inequalities make both envelopes equal \(q_s\) at each observed date. Hence their values simultaneously satisfy all cross-date restrictions. This is stronger than separately reporting a feasible interval at each date.

Since the health target uses nonnegative discount weights, the exact beneficiary-level completion interval is
\[
\left[\sum_{t\in\mathcal T}\beta^t\ell_t,\
      \sum_{t\in\mathcal T}\beta^tu_t\right].
\tag{C}
\]
Both endpoints are attained by the corresponding full trajectory. Convex mixtures of those trajectories obey (A) and attain intermediate totals. The same conclusion holds at \(L=0\): all live indices must coincide with any observed value, or may take a common arbitrary value if none is observed.

Let \(L_a^L,U_a^L\) be the regime-specific population expectations of the endpoints in (C), using the source's fixed cohort weights and identified observed-data law. Selecting the lower or upper envelope separately for each observed history is measurable in this finite horizon. These choices preserve every observed variable, including survival, utilization and travel. With no additional cross-beneficiary or cross-regime health restrictions, the sharp health contrast is
\[
\Delta H\in[L_1^L-U_0^L,\ U_1^L-L_0^L].
\]
Combining with the source's common unit-resource-cost class gives the sharp welfare interval
\[
\left[
\lambda(L_1^L-U_0^L)-\rho\Delta T-h_{\mathcal C}(\Delta Q),\
\lambda(U_1^L-L_0^L)-\rho\Delta T+h_{\mathcal C}(-\Delta Q)
\right].
\tag{D}
\]
Sharpness uses the source's independence between health completions and the shared cost-vector restriction. If scientific restrictions link latent health to utilization, further joint feasibility work is required.

For example, an observed live score \(q_2=0.8\) and bound \(L=0.1\) restrict a missing live year-three score to \([0.7,0.9]\), rather than \([0,1]\); other observed years may tighten it further through (B). This is an illustrative envelope calculation, not a clinical assertion about actual annual quality changes.

The extension supplies an exact sensitivity family indexed by a declared trajectory bound. It does not validate that bound, identify acquisition assignment, or infer mediation from the ownership-payment factorial. It preserves the cohort across moves and death and makes no empirical or medical recommendation.
